extracted.intended_audience: college mathematics instructors / mathematics teacher educators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for facilitating discussion-rich, equitable, and productive mathematics classroom talk (asking questions, managing participation, and elevating student thinking). Targets instructors seeking to improve discussion practices in college math courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academically productive talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk that focuses on helping students recognize, build on, and respond to the thinking of the teacher and their peers; supports deeper student reasoning and the expression of that reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use talk that supports students to engage in meaningful mathematical discussions at higher levels (beyond mere recall). Productive talk increases learning and student participation; teacher support for it mediates the connection between participation and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Initiate-Response-Evaluation (IRE) pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: The IRE sequence (Initiate (Teacher) → Response (Student) → Evaluation (Teacher)) produces low-level, bite-sized conversations that rarely involve student-to-student interaction and contain little mathematical substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and avoid defaulting to quickly telling students whether answers are right or wrong; instead elicit and build on student ideas so conversation involves peers and deeper reasoning. Example IRE: Teacher: 'What do we put here in the equation?' Student: 'x3.' Teacher: 'Actually, it is x4.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask authentic, non-evaluative questions to elicit student thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions should aim to elicit student ideas (not immediate evaluation) so students articulate thinking aloud; this reveals student thinking and invites participation beyond correct answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prompts such as 'How are you thinking about this problem?', 'What are your initial ideas about this?', 'Where are you getting stuck?', 'Does this look like anything we’ve done before?', and 'What are you wondering about that would help you make progress?'. These help learn what students know and broaden participation, especially for historically disenfranchised students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite students to comment on peers' thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Use peer-comment questions after short partner or group discussions to allow students to share ideas without taking sole ownership, lessening fear of failure and inviting participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample prompts: 'What was something interesting that your peer shared with you?', 'Did you get any new ideas from your partner?', 'Was there any place where the two of you got stuck?', 'What did you and your partner wonder about?', 'Can someone tell me what your group talked about?', 'Did your group have a consensus, or did you have different ideas?'. Implement after think-pair-share or turn-and-talk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use active listening and nonjudgmental acknowledgments
rubrics_metrics.description: When student thinking becomes public, respond first with active listening cues and non-evaluative acknowledgments rather than immediate judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonverbal cues: eye contact, nodding, open posture. Verbal acknowledgments: 'That’s interesting, thanks for sharing.', 'You mentioned X, and I would love if you could explain more about that.', 'Could you tell me more about…?', 'All right, is there anything else?', 'I wonder how what you’re saying connects to…', 'Does anyone have any questions for our speaker?', 'Would anybody else like to add on?', 'Can somebody else explain that idea in their own words?'. These further conversation and create a conversation-rich environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address incorrect ideas without shutting down discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: When students offer incorrect or incomplete reasoning, avoid curt factual shut-downs; instead use follow-ups that reveal misconceptions while preserving participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Rather than saying 'No, that’s not correct at all,' respond with 'That’s interesting, but how can you be sure that you’ve covered all of the cases?' Then invite others: 'Does anyone else have any other ideas?' Use the exchange to learn about misunderstandings (e.g., incomplete grasp of induction) and eventually make clear that the empirical argument was flawed while maintaining a safe environment for sharing. Use direct correction sparingly and only when classroom norms allow it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize process over binary right/wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses that emphasize process, ways of thinking, and productive missteps encourage students to see mathematics as a process rather than only correct answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize process-focused discourse to support productive struggle and failure; avoid reinforcing the idea that math is only about getting the right answer, which discourages risk-taking and collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: What–How–Why question hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: A hierarchy for categorizing teacher questions: what (recall/product), how (process), why (justification/explanation), plus an other category for logistics and participation prompts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this hierarchy (adopted in the EQUIP tool) to increase awareness of question types and move instruction toward more how and why questions. Teachers often overuse what questions (sometimes 80%+); aim for less than 50% what questions as a practical target in professional development (not a strict research-based cutoff).

rubrics_metrics.name: What questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions that focus on providing an answer or recalling a fact; aligned with 'math is about getting the right answer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'What did you get for number 4?', 'Can someone tell me what the answer is?', 'Do we have an example of where that’s not true?', 'Do you remember the definition of a limit?' Frequent use reinforces answer-focused culture and de-emphasizes process; reduce their proportion in classroom questioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: How questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions that focus on the process a student followed to get an answer; they invite multiple valid approaches and expose different student thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'How are you thinking about this problem?', 'How did you get started?', 'Can you tell me how you did this problem?', 'What was your process for solving the problem?' Use these to compare approaches (e.g., direct proof vs. contradiction) and to surface diverse ways of thinking. They are underused and valuable for building conceptual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions aiming for justification or explanation that press students to engage in sensemaking and theory building; generally the deepest question type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Can you explain what you figured out?', 'Can somebody tell the class why this works?', 'Why do you need an exponent in this equation?', 'How do you know that seven is the correct answer?' Use why questions to develop explanation and justification skills. Be mindful of equity: why questions are often disproportionately asked of already-privileged students, concentrating high-status talk; intentionally support and scaffold other students to engage at why-level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other question types (logistics/participation prompts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions that manage logistics, participation, or invite meta-commentary rather than mathematical content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Do you understand?', 'Do you agree?', 'What questions do you have?', 'What comments do you have for the speaker?', 'Is there anything you want to know more about?', 'Can someone repeat what Brenda just said?' Use these to organize participation and to get students to build on each other’s ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deepen questions / Teacher press (sequencing follow-ups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategies to move from what → how → why using follow-up questions (teacher press) to elicit deeper reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write down questions ahead of time or plan follow-ups; use what/how as leads into why. Example sequence: 'What answers did people get for #4?' → 'How did you get to that answer?' → 'How do you know that’s correct?' You may also jump directly to how or why. Regular use trains students to expect justification and explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about participation management
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell students why and how you are managing participation (e.g., why you want raising hands, the goal of getting a variety of ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model and explain strategies (e.g., give think time, instruct turn-and-talk). If students don’t respond, explicitly invite more time and try partner discussion: 'Hey, this is important and I’m going to give you plenty of time to think about it...' or 'Please turn to a partner and discuss for two minutes, and then I’ll ask the class again.' Clear communication helps normalize norms and equity goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use body placement to manage attention
rubrics_metrics.description: How and where you position yourself in the room communicates expectations and helps manage participation and attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move around the room to listen in on small groups, stand at a table to elevate a group's idea, or stand near disruptive tables to quiet them nonverbally. Body placement signals engagement and allows strategic checking-in with students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require and use hand raising
rubrics_metrics.description: Using hand raising as the default turn-taking mechanism increases equity and prevents dominance by quick or loud students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why hand raising is used and enforce it early; do not allow shouting out answers as the norm. Hand raising broadens participation and mitigates reproduction of societal inequities in classroom interactions. Exceptions may exist but should be rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor controls calling on students; interrupt dominant students
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish that the instructor will call on students to ensure equitable turn-taking and to prevent a few students from dominating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use polite but firm language to redirect dominant students (examples provided: 'I see that you’re really interested... but I’d like to hear from others', 'Please wait, we’ll get to you in a moment'). Remind students about the value of multiple voices and be prepared to interrupt to protect classroom equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wait time (before calling and after student talk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberately pause before calling on students and after a student speaks to allow thinking and processing; increases diversity and quality of responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count silently to 10 before calling on anyone; explicitly explain this to students as a norm. Wait after student responses to allow others to process and to emphasize important comments. Introduce it as research-based practice and normalize the 'art of awkwardness'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple Hands strategy (e.g., five hands)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wait for multiple students to raise hands (e.g., five) before calling on someone to ensure think time and broaden participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell students you will wait for five hands and then choose anyone to speak (first, fifth, or someone who didn’t raise a hand). This guarantees more students had time to think and enables gentle invitations to quieter students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think–Pair–Share and Turn-and-Talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Short cycles of individual think time, partner discussion, and whole-class share (think-pair-share) or immediate partner talk (turn-and-talk) to increase access to participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep think times brief (under a minute) and pair discussions short (a couple minutes). Use these when whole-class silence occurs; while powerful, manage the share portion to avoid reintroducing inequities or undue stress (e.g., cold calling). Consider virtual adaptations (breakout rooms). Obtain student consent during pair work before public sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting students strategically to broaden participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Select who to call on based on knowledge of participation inequities and local data to intentionally bring in under-participating students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect local data (see Chapter 7) and include names of less-participatory students in lesson plans to remind yourself to involve them. If many students from minoritized groups avoid participating, use stronger facilitation (assigning competence, orchestrating discussions) or address classroom climate issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assigning competence (elevating student status)
rubrics_metrics.description: An instructor strategy to draw positive attention to student ideas intentionally to disrupt hierarchies and elevate the status of students perceived as low status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three components: (1) identify a student perceived as low status (use data), (2) identify their mathematical contribution, and (3) make that contribution public. Use facilitation strategies to elicit contributions and monitor participation until an appropriate contribution appears; then publicly value it to raise the student's status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spotlight (making contributions public)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific assigning-competence strategy: pause to highlight a particular student's contribution so it is valued and others can learn from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases: 'I want to pause for a minute while you think about that idea,' 'I heard something really interesting in the partner share that I want you all to hear,' 'I’d like you all to think about Alyssa’s argument.' Avoid spotlighting incorrect ideas to prevent embarrassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming ideas (attach student name to idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attach a student's name to an idea (e.g., 'Katy’s conjecture') to create a durable association and elevate the student's status through recurring recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when an idea or approach is useful and you want the class to focus on it or return to it later. Be careful not to only name ideas of high-status students; naming should support equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher press (as part of assigning competence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use follow-up questions to ask a student to explain more of their thinking, moving them along the what–how–why continuum and drawing attention to their competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press surface-level responses (e.g., 'I got four') with deeper prompts to reveal process and reasoning. Use prior knowledge from turn-and-talk or small-group work to press students at appropriate times. Monitor whether press gives positive attention or exposes confusion and adjust accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revoice
rubrics_metrics.description: A facilitation move referenced as the next strategy (revoice) to make student thinking public and clear by restating or reframing student contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as a strategy following teacher press; text chunk ends before detailed guidance. Generally, revoicing typically involves the teacher restating a student's idea to clarify meaning and invite confirmation or extension.
